comment: Validation oracles: the published specifications whose own examples are the Prism's test content. tools/oracle/gen.py fetches each source at its pinned SHA-256, takes its examples out mechanically (an example is kept only if every address in it is at a domain reserved for documentation, RFC 2606 and RFC 6761, so no real person's address enters the repository), and reads each one with a reference reader written to the source's own grammar. test/oracle/read.test.mjs then holds the Prism's reading (site/card.mjs readItem) to that reading, field by field: a message's title, sender, time and plain words; an event's title, place and start; a card's name; a header's encoded words as the specification says they display; a base64 test vector as it decodes; a CSV example as RFC 4180 reads it; a one-time code message as the WICG report says; an element's accessible name as W3C AccName computes it, graded in the browser on the Web Platform Tests' own cases (test/oracle/name.test.mjs); the items a page shows, read as W3C's own feed example renders them, each article heard by its name; an urgency or scarcity line, as the researchers who found it labelled it, as coercive. gaps: kinds of content the Prism reads that no published specification gives examples of, each with why; no test content is written for them. label: the kind of thing a source's specification says its whole messages and events are (a kind the kind reader names); unsourced: kinds no specification publishes a whole example of, each with why. Nothing here is invented: a new kind of content is added by naming the specification it follows. classifications: the published classifications the Prism's own models are made of rather than tested with, each pinned the same way and generated in full into the page by its own generator (the whole-person model, tools/person/gen.py, from WHO's ICF release); each is a cited authority whose evidence is the generator's gate, with the licence it is used under, and gaps: what the classification has that its machine-readable release does not carry.

sources.comment: What a line asks of its reader, as AMI's annotators marked each dialogue act. Its classes are the general-purpose communicative functions of ISO 24617-2 (Bunt et al.): Inform provides information (a fact); the Elicit acts seek it (a question); Suggest is a directive and Offer a commissive, both an action someone is to take (a task). Backchannels, stalls, fragments, assessments and social acts ask nothing of the owner and are not mapped. train: the series of AMI's scenario training partition, whose acts the intent head is fit on (test/oracle/intent.test.mjs, INTENT_FIT); they never enter the repository, only the head's weights do.

sources.held: DialogBank's pages state no licence, and its dialogues come from corpora with terms of their own (Switchboard, HCRC Map Task, TRAINS, DBOX, the Hujiang lessons). Its files are pinned; no word of them is committed, only how many acts they gave and their SHA-256. No gate downloads them, so nothing here is enforced where the Prism is built: the source is read only with --fetch, and test/oracle/intent.test.mjs reads it only when DIALOGUE_HELD names the acts tools/oracle/gen.py --fetch --held wrote, and says so when it does not.

acts that accept, decline or address a request, a suggestion or an offer are commissives or directives whose content is the act they depend on; without functional dependence the reader cannot say what is committed to, so they are not mapped onto an intent
certainty, conditionality and sentiment qualifiers; the Prism reads none

sources.comment: What each functional segment of a dialogue does, in every dimension, and which earlier acts it depends on, as ISO 24617-2's own editors annotated it. acts: the standard's general-purpose functions onto the router's intents, in the task dimension: the information-seeking functions a question, the information-providing functions a fact, the directives and the commissives that open an action (instruct, request, suggest, offer, promise) a task. malformed: files that are not well-formed XML as published (a <when> element left unclosed); they are pinned and not read, and nothing is repaired. unenforced: what the annotation carries that no reader of the Prism is yet held to, each with why; test/oracle/intent.test.mjs counts each where the acts are supplied. measured: what the intent reader found on the acts, when and where; a measurement, not a threshold any gate holds.

gaps.why: How often a source writes is measured by site/time/rhythm.mjs, which is held to the instances RFC 5545 section 3.8.5.3 lists for its recurrence rules (test/time/rhythm.test.mjs). No pinned specification gives several messages from one sender that keep a cycle (RFC 5322 Appendix A has at most three times from one sender), and a public mailing-list archive would bring real people's timing into the repository, which the no-PII rule keeps out even with names replaced. So the chat's sentence for such a sender is tested only on a rhythm handed to it, until a specification publishes such an exchange.

No published specification gives example card numbers: ISO/IEC 7812-1, which defines the issuer prefix and the Luhn check digit, is not freely published, and the networks' test numbers are on their own changing pages. The card detector (site/google/ingest.mjs) has no oracle test until one is pinned.
WhatsApp publishes no definition of its Export chat text format, only help pages on how to export. site/source/exports.mjs reads it, untested by any oracle.

Discord's help pages name the files of a data package (messages/index.json, messages/c<id>/messages.json or .csv) but publish no definition of their fields. Untested by any oracle; its CSV files follow RFC 4180, which is.
LinkedIn's help pages name messages.csv and Connections.csv but publish no definition of their columns. Untested by any oracle; the files follow RFC 4180, which is.

The senses guest (app/src/PrismSenses.lex.tex) is held to W3C's SOSA ontology and the Recommendation's example graphs through its 'check' verb. Its 'observe' and 'flat' verbs, which answer the person's circumstances at a prompt, have no acceptance vector: no source gives the expected observations, and the model's own output is not an oracle. app/specs/senses/spec.json 'gaps' names the oracle each expected observation is to be derived from (IANA tz test data, RFC 3339, RFC 5545 at a pinned clock, RFC 6350, WHO ICF, Geolocation WPT).

gaps.kind: a Web Annotation Set with no id
gaps.why: The annotation-model suite (app/specs/annotation/spec.json) fails the Recommendation's own Examples 42 to 44 on 3.2-targetObjectsRecognized: a Composite, List or Independents with no id, which section 3.2.8 allows. The annotation guest answers as the suite does until the suite is corrected upstream.

gaps.kind: what a Web Annotation selector selects
gaps.why: The suite tests an annotation's shape only. No published test says what a selector or a refinedBy chain selects in a text, so resolving a citation's selector has no oracle yet.
